overview: GSK is a UK-headquartered global biopharma company that discovers, develops and commercializes specialty medicines, vaccines and general medicines, organized around four core therapeutic areas: respiratory/immunology & inflammation (RI&I), oncology, HIV and infectious diseases. The company demerged its Consumer Healthcare business as Haleon in July 2022 to become a focused biopharma pure-play, and now generates sales of roughly £32-33bn/year across the US, Europe and International markets, reporting in GBP despite the majority of sales being denominated in USD and other currencies. GSK holds leading positions in HIV (via its ~78%-owned ViiV Healthcare joint venture), herpes zoster (shingles) and meningitis vaccines, and a growing oncology and respiratory biologics franchise, while its General Medicines segment (Trelegy, legacy respiratory and antibiotics) is in managed decline.

business_model.summary: GSK earns revenue from product sales of patented/branded specialty medicines and vaccines (high margin, R&D- and patent-protected) and older general medicines (lower growth, facing generic/biosimilar and pricing pressure). Specialty Medicines (HIV, RI&I, oncology) is the primary growth engine (+14% CER in Q2 2026), Vaccines is a large, high-margin, seasonally-weighted franchise (Shingrix, meningitis, RSV), and General Medicines (Trelegy, legacy respiratory, established antibiotics) is declining due to generic competition, Medicare Part D redesign and pricing pressure. Revenue is transactional (product/dose sales, government tenders, insurance/PBM reimbursement) rather than subscription-based, though chronic therapies (HIV, biologics) and recurring vaccination programs provide repeat-purchase dynamics. ViiV Healthcare (HIV) is majority GSK-owned with Pfizer and Shionogi as minority partners, consolidated into GSK's HIV sales line.

revenue_streams.name: Vaccines (Shingrix, Meningitis, Arexvy, paediatric)
revenue_streams.trend: growing (+6-8% CER YTD 2026, Shingrix/RSV facing competition)

business_model.customer_type: B2B/B2G - national health systems, government tenders and public health bodies (Gavi, CDC, UK NHS, EU procurement) for vaccines; insurers, PBMs, hospitals and specialist physicians for medicines; ultimately prescribed to/used by individual patients (B2C end-demand)
business_model.geographic_mix: US ~50% of turnover (£8.0bn YTD H1 2026 of £16.0bn), Europe ~26% (£4.1bn), International ~24% (£3.9bn); heavy USD/EUR revenue translated into GBP reporting currency creates significant FX translation exposure

competitive_position.market_position: Global leader in HIV treatment/prevention (ViiV, ~90%+ of long-acting injectable HIV market via Cabenuva/Apretude) and a top-3 global vaccines manufacturer (#1 or #2 in shingles and meningitis vaccines); smaller, more diversified positions in oncology (ADCs, PARP inhibitors) and respiratory biologics (Nucala) versus larger pharma peers.

moat_factors.factor: HIV franchise scale and long-acting injectable (LAI) lead
moat_factors.description: ViiV/GSK pioneered long-acting injectable HIV treatment (Cabenuva) and prevention (Apretude, cabotegravir-based), which delivered 80% of HIV growth in Q2 2026; LAIs create high switching costs/compliance advantages versus daily oral regimens and face limited near-term LAI competition.

One of the broadest vaccine portfolios in the industry (33 manufacturing sites, decades of adjuvant/platform expertise e.g. AS01), supporting Shingrix's continued global uptake (US immunisation only ~45%) and new launches (Arexvy, Penmenvy).

moat_factors.factor: Patent/regulatory exclusivity on branded specialty medicines
moat_factors.description: FDA/EMA-protected exclusivity on Nucala, Jemperli, Ojjaara/Omjjara, Benlysta and Blenrep supports premium pricing, though protection is time-limited and subject to loss-of-exclusivity (LoE) cliffs.

moat_factors.factor: Brand/relationship with payers and health systems
moat_factors.description: Long-standing relationships with governments (Gavi, CDC, NHS) and large-scale tender/contract manufacturing capability provide an edge in vaccine supply agreements versus smaller biotechs.

moat_factors.factor: R&D pipeline depth and AI-enabled discovery
moat_factors.description: 62 assets in clinical development (19 in phase III) and recent bolt-on M&A (Nuvalent, Alteogen, RAPT, Noetik) aim to sustain pipeline productivity, though large pharma peers (Pfizer, Merck, AstraZeneca) have comparable or larger R&D budgets.

weaknesses: Heavy reliance on dolutegravir-based HIV products (~£2.7bn of H1 2026 sales) facing loss of exclusivity in the US from April 2028 and the EU from mid-2029, a well-flagged but large patent cliff
General Medicines in structural decline (Trelegy hurt by US Medicare Part D redesign, channel mix pricing pressure and generic erosion across legacy respiratory/antibiotics)
Camlipixant (chronic cough) programme terminated in July 2026 after missing Phase III endpoints, resulting in a ~£1.3bn impairment - a reminder of binary late-stage pipeline risk
Arexvy (RSV) losing share to Pfizer's Abrysvo and facing Moderna's mRESVIA, in a vaccine category with lower-than-expected uptake industry-wide
GBP reporting currency against predominantly USD/EUR cash flows creates reported-results volatility independent of underlying operating performance

growth_drivers: Specialty Medicines launch cycle: Exdensur (severe asthma, ultra-long-acting biologic), Blenrep (multiple myeloma ADC), Blujepa (first-in-class oral antibiotic for uUTI/gonorrhoea) and Penmenvy (5-in-1 meningococcal vaccine) all approved/launching in 2025-2026

Oncology pipeline acceleration via the Nuvalent acquisition (~$10.6bn, closed July 2026) adding zidesamtinib (ROS1) and neladalkib (ALK) for non-small cell lung cancer, plus Jemperli, Ojjaara/Omjjara and Blenrep organic growth

'Accelerate Growth' 3-year programme (announced July 2026) targeting 20+ phase III trial starts in 2026 (up from a prior plan of 10) and £1.9bn of annual run-rate savings by 2029 to fund reinvestment in R&D and protect margins through the dolutegravir loss-of-exclusivity window (2028-2030)
HIV long-acting injectables (Cabenuva, Apretude) continuing double-digit growth, with YTD 2026 LAI sales exceeding £1bn and representing 35% of US HIV turnover
Vaccines runway: Shingrix international expansion (ex-US immunisation rates still only ~12% in GSK's 10 priority ex-US markets vs 45% in the US) and Arexvy label expansion opportunities

2031 risk-adjusted sales outlook of more than £40bn (raised from £38bn in Feb 2025), with management stating ~90% of that ambition already approved or launching within three years, and accelerating growth expected beyond 2031

Targeted bolt-on business development (Nuvalent, Alteogen, RAPT Therapeutics, Noetik and others - 14 new partnerships/acquisitions in 2025) to supplement organic pipeline in oncology, respiratory, immunology and infectious disease

business.description: Core HIV franchise (Tivicay, Triumeq, Dovato - dolutegravir-based) generated ~£2.7bn in H1 2026 sales; US exclusivity loss from ~April 2028 and EU from mid-2029 threatens a large, high-margin revenue base, though ViiV's newer LAI portfolio (Cabenuva, Apretude) is intended to offset this.

Camlipixant's Phase III CALM-1/CALM-2 failure in chronic cough (July 2026) triggered a ~£1.3bn impairment, illustrating binary downside risk inherent in late-stage pipeline bets; GSK's 2031 outlook and Accelerate Growth plan depend on numerous similarly binary approvals.

Arexvy (RSV) is losing US market share to Pfizer's Abrysvo and facing Moderna's mRESVIA; Shingrix faces slower-than-hoped international uptake and periodic US demand softness/channel inventory effects.

Trelegy and other legacy respiratory/antibiotic products are shrinking (-7 to -9% CER YTD 2026) due to US Medicare Part D redesign, channel-mix pricing pressure and generic competition, acting as a drag on consolidated growth.

New CEO Luke Miels (former Chief Commercial Officer) took over from Emma Walmsley at end of 2025/into 2026, alongside a major reorganisation (Accelerate Growth) - transition and restructuring execution risk persists.

financial.description: GSK reports in GBP while the majority of sales are in USD/EUR; management estimates that if July 2026 exchange rates held for the rest of the year, Sterling turnover growth would be cut by 2 percentage points and Core Operating Profit growth by 4 points - a strengthening pound is a direct headwind to reported results.

Total operating profit fell 75% and EPS 69% in Q2 2026 due to the camlipixant impairment and Accelerate Growth restructuring charges (£2.4bn total cost, £2.1bn cash, mostly in 2026-2027), creating large swings between Total and Core (non-IFRS) results that can obscure underlying trends.
2026 guidance flags higher interest charges of ~£800m (including Nuvalent acquisition financing) and a rising effective tax rate (~17.5%), both headwinds to EPS growth even as operating profit grows.

regulatory.risk: US drug pricing reform / MFN agreement
regulatory.description: GSK (and ViiV) signed a Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) pricing and tariff-exemption agreement with the US Administration (December 2025, finalized April 2026) exchanging lower US prices on certain medicines/Medicaid access for a three-year exemption from Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs; terms are not fully public and Congressional Democrats have questioned the actual consumer benefit, leaving residual uncertainty on pricing/tariff treatment beyond 2029.

GSK settled roughly 80,000 (93%) of US state-court Zantac (ranitidine) cancer-claim cases for up to $2.2bn in October 2024, with implementation targeted for H1 2025; remaining cases outside that settlement and other Zantac-related claims (including from co-defendants Sanofi, Pfizer and Boehringer Ingelheim) could still create future liability, legal cost or reputational exposure for GSK.

Pharmaceutical-specific tariffs remain a live US trade-policy tool; GSK's tariff relief is tied to the MFN agreement and conditioned on continued compliance, so a change in US trade policy stance could reintroduce tariff cost exposure.

US Medicare Part D redesign (post-Inflation Reduction Act) and channel-mix pricing adjustments are already denting Trelegy and other General Medicines sales, and could extend to future Specialty Medicines pricing and reimbursement negotiations.

macro.description: Higher-for-longer rates raise financing costs on GSK's debt (including new Nuvalent-related borrowing), though the company maintains strong free cash flow (£4.0bn in 2025) and investment-grade credit profile.

Management explicitly cites a 'dynamic' geopolitical operating landscape and US trade/tariff policy as requiring agile leadership; supply chain and manufacturing footprint (33 sites across multiple countries) carries some concentration and cross-border risk.
International segment sales (~24% of turnover) carry emerging-market currency and payment risk alongside the broader USD/EUR-to-GBP translation effect.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global biopharma industry outlook remains supportive of mid-single-digit volume growth driven by aging populations, rising chronic disease burden and continued vaccine uptake, but is increasingly shaped by government pricing intervention (US MFN deals, IRA-style reforms, EU reference pricing) and major incumbents' simultaneous patent cliffs (GSK's dolutegravir, alongside peers' own LoE events).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low to moderate - pharmaceutical/vaccine demand is largely non-discretionary and defensive relative to the broader economy, though vaccine uptake (discretionary adult immunisation) and hospital/elective procedure volumes can show some sensitivity to healthcare budgets and consumer willingness to seek care.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low to moderate direct sensitivity given strong free cash flow generation, but rising rates increase financing costs on acquisition debt (e.g., Nuvalent) and discount rates used in impairment testing of intangible pipeline assets.
key_input_costs: Active pharmaceutical ingredients and biologics manufacturing inputs
Contract manufacturing and third-party supply costs

recent_developments.event: GSK (and ViiV Healthcare) signed a Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) drug pricing agreement with the US Administration, trading US price concessions and Medicaid access commitments for a three-year exemption from Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs; the definitive agreement was finalised 9 April 2026 with Generous Model Manufacturer Participation Agreements signed effective 15 June 2026.

Luke Miels (previously Chief Commercial Officer) formally became CEO, succeeding Emma Walmsley who stepped down at end of 2025 after transforming GSK through the Haleon demerger and a re-set balance sheet.

FY2025 annual results: turnover up 7% CER to £32.7bn, core operating profit +11% CER to £9.8bn, core EPS +12% to 172.0p, free cash flow £4.0bn, full-year dividend of 66p (up from 61p); five major FDA/EMA/Japan approvals in 2025 including Blenrep for multiple myeloma.

GSK agreed to acquire Nuvalent, Inc. for $124/share cash (~$10.6bn equity value, ~$9.4bn net of cash) to add clinical-stage lung-cancer oncology assets zidesamtinib (ROS1) and neladalkib (ALK); deal closed 15 July 2026.

GSK discontinued development of camlipixant for chronic cough after Phase III CALM-1/CALM-2 trials missed primary and secondary endpoints, resulting in a ~£1.3-1.9bn impairment charge recognised in Q2 2026 results (retaining a smaller carrying value tied to a potential IBS indication).

Q2 2026 results: total turnover +5% CER to £8.4bn (YTD £16.0bn +5%), core operating profit +7% CER, core EPS +9% CER; total operating profit -75% and total EPS -69% due to the camlipixant impairment and higher restructuring charges; 2026 full-year CER guidance reaffirmed (turnover +3-5%, core OP +7-9%, core EPS +7-9%), with turnover/core OP guided to the upper half and core EPS to the lower half of ranges; completed the £2bn share buyback programme announced at FY2024 results.

Launched a new 3-year 'Accelerate Growth' restructuring programme targeting £1.9bn of annual savings by 2029 (£2.4bn total cost, £2.1bn cash) to fund R&D reinvestment and protect margins through the 2028-2030 dolutegravir loss-of-exclusivity window; raised 2026 phase III trial-start guidance to 20+ (from 10) and announced a new flagship R&D Centre on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, UK.

Continued implementation of the ~$2.2bn Zantac (ranitidine) settlement covering ~80,000 (93%) of US state-court product-liability cases, alongside a separate ~$70m Valisure qui tam settlement pending final DOJ approval; residual/uncovered claims remain outstanding.
Early-2026 bolt-on deals (Noetik, RAPT Therapeutics, Alteogen) added to the pipeline, continuing a pattern of 14 new partnerships/acquisitions disclosed for 2025.

items.notes: Specialty Medicines expected to grow at a low double-digit percentage; Vaccines broadly stable to low single-digit growth (upgraded from prior decline-to-stable guide); General Medicines to decline mid-to-low single digit (worse than prior guide of low single-digit decline to stable).

items.vs_prior: maintained range, narrowed to upper half
items.notes: Driven by gross margin leverage from Specialty Medicines mix and operational efficiencies; SG&A now expected broadly stable; R&D expected to grow significantly ahead of sales as Accelerate Growth investment ramps; royalty income guided to £850-900m.

items.notes: Reflects higher interest charges (~£800m, including Nuvalent financing) and a rising effective tax rate (~17.5%), partly offset by the benefit of the completed £2bn share buyback.
Management states ~90% of the ambition comes from products already approved or planned to launch within three years; accelerating growth is expected from 2031 onwards.

items.notes: Dependent on successful execution of the Accelerate Growth cost programme and new product launches offsetting the HIV patent cliff.

items.target: £1.9 billion annual run-rate savings by 2029, for total costs of £2.4bn (£2.1bn cash)
items.notes: Savings primarily to be reinvested in R&D/business development, with a portion used to support operating margin during the dolutegravir loss-of-exclusivity period; majority of cost charges expected in 2026 and 2027.
Reflects 7 identified late-stage asset accelerations across 18 indications in Oncology, Respiratory, Hepatology and Vaccines.

items.target: 70p expected for full year 2026 (17p declared for Q2 2026)
items.notes: Dividend policy and expected pay-out ratio unchanged; GSK completed its £2bn share buyback programme (announced at FY2024 results) in Q2 2026.

items.notes: Illustrates GSK's GBP-reporting sensitivity to a stronger pound against USD/EUR/JPY.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Luke Miels: 'GSK has delivered another quarter of strong core results performance, with our key growth drivers performing well. We remain focused on operational delivery, execution, and accelerating R&D.' Management reiterated confidence in the >£40bn 2031 sales outlook ('the number 40 is doable, and I stand behind it' - Miels) and framed the Accelerate Growth restructuring and accelerated R&D pipeline (20+ phase III starts) as the mechanism to offset the 2028-2030 dolutegravir loss-of-exclusivity headwind while sustaining margins and shareholder returns.

bull_case: Market-leading, high-margin HIV franchise (via ViiV) with long-acting injectables (Cabenuva, Apretude) delivering sustained double-digit growth and high switching costs, providing a credible offset to the well-telegraphed dolutegravir patent cliff (2028-2030)

Broad, well-funded late-stage pipeline (62 assets, 19 in Phase III, 20+ trial starts planned for 2026) bolstered by disciplined bolt-on M&A (Nuvalent in oncology, plus Alteogen, RAPT, Noetik), supporting a credible path to the >£40bn 2031 sales outlook, ~90% of which is already approved or near-term launch-ready

New 'Accelerate Growth' cost programme (£1.9bn annual savings by 2029) is explicitly designed to protect margins through the HIV patent cliff while funding reinvestment in R&D, addressing the market's biggest structural concern

Strong, growing free cash flow (£4.0bn in 2025, up from £2.9bn in 2024) supports a rising dividend (70p guided for 2026, up from 66p) and completed share buybacks, with a reset, de-risked balance sheet following the 2022 Haleon demerger

Vaccines and Specialty Medicines franchises (Shingrix international expansion still early-stage at ~12% ex-US immunisation, growing Nucala/Benlysta/Jemperli/Blenrep oncology and immunology sales) offer multiple avenues of growth independent of the HIV patent cliff
bear_case: Dolutegravir-based HIV products (~£2.7bn of H1 2026 sales, a large share of high-margin Specialty Medicines) face loss of exclusivity in the US from 2028 and EU from 2029, and replacement growth from LAIs and new launches is not guaranteed to fully offset the resulting revenue/margin cliff

Binary late-stage pipeline risk is real and recently realized: camlipixant's July 2026 Phase III failure triggered a ~£1.3-1.9bn impairment, and GSK's ambitious 2031 outlook depends on numerous similarly binary trial outcomes across its pipeline

General Medicines (Trelegy and legacy respiratory/antibiotics, ~31% of turnover) is in structural decline (-7 to -9% CER) from US Medicare Part D redesign, channel pricing pressure and generic erosion, acting as a persistent drag on consolidated growth

US drug-pricing policy (MFN agreement, Section 232 tariff exposure, ongoing Congressional scrutiny) and residual Zantac litigation create regulatory/legal overhang with terms and ultimate cost not fully transparent or finalized

GBP reporting currency against predominantly USD/EUR underlying cash flows adds reported-earnings volatility (management's own sensitivity shows a stronger pound cutting Core Operating Profit growth by up to 4 points), and vaccine franchises (Arexvy, and potentially Shingrix) face intensifying competition from Pfizer and Moderna
